lessons.title: Types and Causes of Sports Injuries

before.content_html:
Acute vs Chronic Injuries

Sports injuries fall into two fundamental categories. Acute injuries are caused by a single sudden traumatic event — a collision, a fall, a missed landing. They have an immediate onset, with pain typically felt instantly. Chronic injuries, by contrast, develop gradually through repetitive movement and overuse; the athlete may notice a dull ache that worsens over weeks or months rather than a sharp pain at a defined moment. Distinguishing these two categories is a foundation of this unit, and the distinction comes up in both short-answer and extended-response exam questions.

Soft Tissue vs Hard Tissue Injuries

Injuries are also classified by which type of body tissue is damaged. Soft-tissue injuries involve muscles, tendons, ligaments, cartilage or skin. Hard-tissue injuries involve bone, including fractures and dislocations. This classification helps to determine treatment: hard-tissue injuries typically require imaging (X-ray) and immobilisation, while soft-tissue injuries may be managed with PRICE therapy and physiotherapy.

Acute Soft-Tissue Injuries: Strains and Sprains

A strain is a tear or overstretching of a muscle or tendon. Strains occur when a muscle is asked to generate force it cannot sustain — for example, a sprinter pulling their hamstring during maximum acceleration, or a weightlifter straining their lower back. Strains are soft-tissue injuries. A sprain, by contrast, is a tear of a ligament — the fibrous tissue that connects bone to bone and stabilises joints. Sprains most commonly affect the ankle, knee and wrist. The most clinically significant ligament in sport is the Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL), located in the knee: ACL injuries typically occur during sudden direction changes, landing from a jump, or deceleration — making them particularly common in football, netball and basketball. Both strains and sprains are acute soft-tissue injuries.

Key Fact

A strain is a torn or overstretched muscle or tendon (soft tissue). A sprain is a torn ligament (soft tissue). The Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) in the knee is the most clinically important ligament in sport science and is commonly injured through sudden twisting or deceleration movements.

Acute Skin Damage: Abrasions, Contusions and Blisters

Skin damage encompasses four types in the specification. Abrasions (grazes) occur when the skin surface is scraped against a hard surface — a rugby player sliding on an artificial pitch or a cyclist falling on a road. Cuts and lacerations involve a break in the skin caused by sharp contact with an implement, a surface or an opponent. Contusions (bruises) result from a direct blow that damages blood vessels beneath the skin without breaking the surface — the bleeding is internal, causing the characteristic discolouration. Blisters are fluid-filled pockets beneath the skin caused by repetitive friction — a rower's hands, a runner's heels and a tennis player's fingers are all common sites. All of these are soft-tissue injuries. They vary in severity: lacerations and contusions can occasionally be serious (a deep laceration may require suturing; a contusion on the head may mask a more serious injury), while abrasions and blisters are typically minor but can become infected if poorly managed.

Acute Hard-Tissue Injuries: Fractures and Dislocations

A fracture is a break in a bone. The specification distinguishes two types. An open (compound) fracture is where the broken bone penetrates through the skin — highly visible, carries a serious infection risk and always requires emergency medical attention. A closed (simple) fracture is where the bone breaks internally without breaking the skin, identified by pain, swelling, deformity and loss of function. A dislocation occurs when the bones of a joint are forced out of their normal anatomical alignment — the shoulder (glenohumeral joint) and fingers are the most commonly dislocated joints in sport. Dislocations are hard-tissue injuries. They typically cause immediate severe pain, a visible deformity and complete loss of normal joint function. Fractures and dislocations must not be manipulated in the field without medical expertise — a suspected fracture or dislocation should be immobilised and the athlete referred immediately to emergency services.

Key Fact

Hard-tissue injuries are limited to fractures (open and closed), stress fractures and dislocations. Every other named injury in the specification — strains, sprains, abrasions, contusions, blisters, concussion, tendonitis, epicondylitis and shin splints — is a soft-tissue injury.

Concussion is a traumatic brain injury caused by a blow or jolt to the head that temporarily disrupts normal brain function. Symptoms include headache, confusion, dizziness, nausea, memory problems and sensitivity to light. The specification requires you to know the possible link between repeated head injuries and the onset of dementia and Alzheimer's disease. This link has become a major safeguarding concern in contact sports, particularly rugby union and American football. Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE) — a degenerative brain condition found post-mortem in former contact sport athletes — is now associated with a history of repeated concussive and sub-concussive blows. As a result, national governing bodies (NGBs) have introduced strict return-to-play protocols: no athlete with suspected concussion should return to play in the same session. Concussion is a soft-tissue injury (brain tissue, not bone).

Chronic injuries develop gradually from repetitive overuse. Tendonitis is inflammation of a tendon caused by repetitive stress. The three named sites are: Achilles tendonitis (posterior heel — common in runners and jumpers); rotator cuff tendonitis (shoulder — common in swimmers, throwers and racket sport players); and patellar tendonitis (knee — common in basketball players and high jumpers, nicknamed "jumper's knee"). Epicondylitis is inflammation of the epicondyle of the humerus (the bony projection at the elbow). Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) causes pain on the outside of the elbow through overuse of the wrist extensor muscles — common in racket sports and repetitive manual tasks. Medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow) causes pain on the inside of the elbow through overuse of the wrist flexors — common in golf, throwing sports and rock climbing. Shin splints (medial tibial stress syndrome) cause pain along the inner shin, typically in runners who rapidly increase their training mileage, run on hard surfaces or have poor footwear. Stress fractures are tiny cracks in bone from repetitive loading — unlike other chronic injuries, they are hard-tissue injuries. All tendonitis, epicondylitis and shin splints are soft-tissue injuries.

lessons.title: Responding to Sports Injuries: First Aid (SALTAPS & PRICE)

before.content_html:
Why First Aid Matters in Sport

Every sports session carries some risk of injury. When something goes wrong, a coach, referee or first aider must act quickly and correctly. Knowing the right assessment and treatment protocols can prevent a minor injury from becoming a serious one, and could even save a life. Two of the most important tools in sport first aid are the SALTAPS protocol and the PRICE therapy framework.

SALTAPS: The On-Field Assessment

SALTAPS is a seven-step routine for assessing an injured performer on the pitch or court. It helps the first responder gather information systematically before deciding whether the athlete can continue, needs to be removed, or requires emergency help. The steps are as follows.

See — observe the incident as it happens or arrive on the scene and look for obvious signs of injury such as unusual posture, swelling or deformity. Ask — question the performer about what happened, where it hurts and what the pain feels like; this gives subjective information that cannot be seen. Look — carry out a visual inspection of the injured area, comparing it to the uninjured side; look for swelling, bruising, redness or deformity. Touch — with the performer’s permission, gently palpate (feel) the area to identify specific points of tenderness or crepitus (a grinding sensation that may indicate a fracture).

Active movement — ask the performer to move the injured part themselves (without assistance) through their pain-free range; this tests whether the muscles and tendons are working. Passive movement — the first aider gently moves the injured joint while the performer’s muscles remain relaxed; this tests the integrity of ligaments and joint structures. Strength testing — the performer resists gentle pressure applied by the first aider; if this is pain-free and strength is maintained, return to play may be considered. If any step reveals a significant problem, the performer should be removed and further assessment arranged.

Key Fact

SALTAPS stands for See, Ask, Look, Touch, Active movement, Passive movement, Strength testing. It is the standard on-field assessment routine used to decide whether an injured performer can continue or must be removed from play.

DRABC: Emergency First Aid

If a performer is unconscious or you suspect a life-threatening emergency, SALTAPS is set aside and the DRABC protocol takes over. Danger — ensure the scene is safe for you, the performer and bystanders before approaching. Response — check for consciousness by calling the performer’s name and tapping their shoulders firmly. Airway — if unresponsive, open the airway by tilting the head back and lifting the chin. Breathing — look, listen and feel for normal breathing for up to 10 seconds. Circulation — if the performer is not breathing normally, call emergency services immediately and begin CPR at 30 chest compressions to 2 rescue breaths.

If a performer is unconscious but breathing normally and has no life-threatening conditions, place them in the recovery position: roll them onto their side, support the head and tilt it back slightly to keep the airway clear, and ensure the top knee is bent to prevent rolling forward. Monitor their breathing continuously until emergency services arrive.

SALTAPS is for alert, conscious performers who have sustained a musculoskeletal injury such as a sprain or strain. The moment a performer is unresponsive, unconscious, not breathing normally, or you suspect cardiac arrest, DRABC must be applied immediately. Never delay DRABC to complete a SALTAPS assessment. The priority order in any emergency is always: safety first, then airway, then circulation. Calling 999 (or 112) early is critical — a defibrillator should be retrieved while CPR begins.

PRICE Therapy: Immediate Soft-Tissue Management

Once a conscious performer with a soft-tissue injury (sprain, strain or contusion) has been assessed and removed from play, PRICE therapy guides the immediate treatment. Applied within the first 24–72 hours, it limits swelling, reduces pain and creates the best conditions for healing.

Protection — protect the injury from further damage, for example by using a splint, sling or by simply stopping the performer from weight-bearing. Rest — stop physical activity to prevent aggravation; this does not mean total bed rest but avoidance of the activity that caused the injury. Ice — apply a cold pack or ice wrapped in a damp cloth for 15–20 minutes every two hours; never apply ice directly to skin as this risks an ice burn. Compression — apply a firm (but not tight) bandage to reduce swelling and provide support. Elevation — raise the injured limb above the level of the heart to reduce blood pooling and oedema.

Key Fact

PRICE stands for Protection, Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation. Each step targets a different aspect of the inflammatory response: protection prevents further damage, ice and compression reduce swelling, and elevation drains excess fluid away from the injury site.

X-rays and Specialist Assessment

When a fracture is suspected following the SALTAPS assessment — for example, if there is point tenderness over bone, obvious deformity or the performer cannot bear weight — the performer must be referred for an X-ray. X-rays detect whether bones are broken and whether a fracture is open or closed. You do not need to understand the technical process of how X-rays work, but you must know that they are the primary imaging tool used to diagnose skeletal injury in sport.

A very common error both in practice and in exam answers is stating that ice should be applied directly to the skin. This causes an ice burn (frostbite injury to the superficial tissues) and is incorrect. Ice must always be wrapped in a damp cloth or placed in an ice bag with a cloth barrier. Similarly, do not state that compression should be applied as tightly as possible — a bandage that is too tight can restrict circulation. If a performer’s fingers or toes become pale, cold or numb after bandaging, the bandage is too tight and must be loosened immediately.

flashcard_questions.a: Coughing, wheezing, shortness of breath and tightness in the chest are the four symptoms listed in the specification.
flashcard_questions.q: What are the four symptoms of asthma?

flashcard_questions.a: Increased ventilation during exercise draws cold, dry air into the airways, causing inflammation and narrowing known as exercise-induced bronchoconstriction.
flashcard_questions.q: What causes an asthma attack during exercise?

flashcard_questions.a: The coach should call 999 immediately, as the asthma attack is severe and requires emergency medical attention.
flashcard_questions.q: What should a coach do if a performer's reliever inhaler has not worked after 10 puffs?

flashcard_questions.a: Type 1: the body cannot produce insulin at all. Type 2: the body does not produce enough insulin, or the insulin produced does not work properly.
flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference in insulin production between Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes?

flashcard_questions.a: Type 2 diabetes is strongly linked to a poor diet and physical inactivity, both of which contribute to insulin resistance over time.
flashcard_questions.q: State two lifestyle factors linked to the development of Type 2 diabetes.

flashcard_questions.a: Increased thirst, urinating more often, extreme tiredness, unexplained weight loss, and cuts that take a long time to heal.
flashcard_questions.q: What are the five common symptoms shared by Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes?

flashcard_questions.a: Hypoglycaemia is dangerously low blood sugar, most often triggered during sport by exercise using up blood glucose faster than it is replaced.
flashcard_questions.q: What is hypoglycaemia and what causes it during a sports session?

flashcard_questions.a: The performer should stop activity and consume fast-acting glucose immediately, such as glucose tablets or a sugary drink.
flashcard_questions.q: How should a hypoglycaemic episode be treated immediately?

flashcard_questions.a: A gradual warm-up raises ventilation slowly, reducing the shock of cold dry air to the airways and lowering the risk of exercise-induced bronchoconstriction.
flashcard_questions.q: Why should a performer with asthma carry out a thorough warm-up before intense exercise?

flashcard_questions.a: Working muscles absorb glucose from the blood for energy during exercise, causing blood sugar levels to drop, which can lead to a hypo.
flashcard_questions.q: Why does exercise lower blood sugar in a Type 1 diabetic performer?

flashcard_questions.a: Hyperglycaemia is high blood sugar (caused by too little insulin or too many carbohydrates), whereas hypoglycaemia is dangerously low blood sugar.
flashcard_questions.q: What is hyperglycaemia and how does it differ from hypoglycaemia?

flashcard_questions.a: A nebuliser converts medication into a fine mist for inhalation, used in severe asthma attacks when a standard inhaler cannot deliver sufficient medication.
flashcard_questions.q: What does a nebuliser do, and when might it be used instead of an inhaler?
